answer: In the Quran 5:21 Moses tells his people to enter the holy land God assigned them; in 5:22-26 they refuse and it is forbidden to them for forty years. 7:137 and 10:93 say God made the oppressed people heirs of blessed lands and settled them in one; 17:104 says to dwell in the land and that He will bring them together at the Hereafter's promise, read by al-Jalalayn as the Hour. None names the land; classical commentators say Syria or Jerusalem. Muslim scholars differ: Atiyyah Saqr of Al-Azhar held the promise lapsed with disobedience, though his fatwa also predicts the Jews will not remain; al-Hussaini and the Jordanian Sheikh al-Adwan hold it unbroken, while Spencer says most Muslims cite other verses against it. Genesis 17:8 gives Canaan to Abraham's descendants 'for an everlasting possession'. Jerusalem and al-Aqsa are sacred in Islam: the Night Journey, the first direction of prayer.

facts.text: Two Muslim voices hold that the Israelites' claim was conditional on obedience or has passed away. Atiyyah Saqr (former head of the Al-Azhar fatwa committee) writes that it stands only while the people obey God; the same fatwa also says that the Jews 'have occupied Palestine, they will never remain there forever' and hopes for 'another defeat and severe blow' at Muslim hands, citing Quran 7:167. An article by Noah Ali Salman on the Jordanian General Iftaa' Department site says the Children of Israel were stripped of 'the honor of the trust' because of their sins and that the earth's 'final outcome belongs to the righteous'; it is framed as seeking clarity on 'the end of the battle between us and the Jews'. A survey by Ersin Çelik finds some contemporary commentators call the land a temporary dwelling during the exodus, not an eternal homeland.

contested.text: How the verses are read is a dispute inside Islam, not between Islam and outsiders. Atiyyah Saqr holds that the promise lasted only while the people obeyed God and no longer exists; Çelik's survey finds that most classical commentators take the holy land to mean Jerusalem and that some contemporary ones call it a temporary dwelling; al-Hussaini reads the Quran as awarding the land to the Jews for all time.

could_not_verify: Whether some Muslims dispute identifying the 'farthest mosque' of 17:1 with Jerusalem: no Muslim source making that argument was found; only the Middle East Quarterly editors' statement that it is 'generally interpreted' as Jerusalem is quoted.
A survey or poll of how many Muslim scholars read the promise as lapsed or as lasting: none found; the card names the scholars it quotes and does not say what share hold either view.

Muhammad Asad and Wahbah al-Zuhayli on 5:21: no readable page found, so not cited. Sayyid Qutb's commentary (read) says the land was 'forbidden to that particular generation' on 'the weightier view'; that is not quoted because it does not address whether the promise lapsed.
The Hamas charter and Spencer's reading of it come from two sites only (Avalon Project and Middle East Quarterly).
The Quran's counter-verses that Saqr cites (21:105, 7:167) and that Jewish readers may expect (7:168) are not quoted from the verse pages.
Al-Hussaini's own essay and Spencer's quotation of him are on one site (Middle East Forum); the second voice, al-Adwan, is known through a news report of an interview, not his own text.
Independent corroboration of Ibn Kathir's reading of 7:137, 10:93 and 17:104: quran.com and alim.org reproduce one abridged text.
not_claimed: That scripture settles a modern political question: who should govern the land, or what borders, is not answered by the verses quoted.
That any reading of these verses is the correct Islamic one; the card reports what the text says and what Muslim scholars have said.
That the Israelites' tie to the land rests on the Quran: Jewish ties rest on Jewish sources and history (see the Jewish presence card).
That Muslim attachment to Jerusalem is weaker or newer because the Quran does not name the city.

skeptic.notes: ROUND TWO. Re-read every new quote with the verses before and after. FIXED by the writer (checked): 5:24 refusal is quoted (the 'powerful people' of 5:22 is not; nit); tafsir on 7:137, 10:93 and 17:104 added and read correctly (Ibn Kathir: Sham; Ibn Kathir/al-Jalalayn: Egypt and Syria; Jalalayn: the Hour, 'all together you and them'); Genesis 17:8 quoted from three translations; Saqr's prediction ('will never remain there forever', 'another defeat') is on the card; Spencer, the Hamas charter, al-Hussaini's own essay and al-Adwan's interview are quoted; the method note left contested. STILL OPEN: (1) facts 11 and 12 have only two sites each (Middle East Forum counted once; Algemeiner; Avalon) so the card is short of three reliable sources, and al-Adwan is known through a news relay of a magazine interview. (2) Facts 6, 7, 8: quran.com and alim.org carry the same abridged Ibn Kathir text, so there are two commentaries (Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn), not three independent ones; the gate counts three sites. (3) Fact 10 headline said 'the promise lapsed' for the Jordanian Iftaa' article, which speaks of the Israelites losing 'the honor of the trust' (carrying the message) and the earth's 'final outcome' going to the righteous; it never discusses 5:21. I reworded the headline to 'conditional on obedience or has passed away'; a better second voice that addresses the land promise is still needed. (4) contested[2]: the quote 'Jerusalem isn't actually mentioned by name' reaches us only through Spencer; I changed the text to say so; al-Hussaini's own essay does not contain it. NEW PROBLEM: the answer still told 17:104 as 'dwell in the land' with no gathering clause, repeating the cut I found in round one; fixed by me. SHOULD-FIX: Genesis 17:8 says 'descendants' with no note that 17:19-21 places the covenant with Isaac, which a Muslim reader will raise; the card's counter-verses (21:105, 7:167-168) are still not quoted from verse pages. Strongest objection from Muslims: two of the three scholars quoted for the lasting reading and the lapsed reading come from the same two sites, and no majority statement from a Muslim source exists (Spencer, a non-Muslim, supplies 'most Muslims'). From Jewish readers: the quoted Muslim voices for the lapsed view are more numerous than for the lasting view.
